prompt: A night-shift astronomer logs a new star that only shines while nobody is looking at it.
Every Thursday the crossing guard at your corner counts one more child than actually walks past. Who is she counting?
The city's lost-and-found office receives an item every morning that you haven't lost yet. Today it's a child's mitten. Whose is it?
The lighthouse logbook has begun recording ships that haven't been built yet, and tonight's entry is your name. Who is writing it?
Every elevator in your building has grown a button for a floor the architect swears doesn't exist, and this morning the doors opened there. Who was waiting?
Your grandmother’s recipe box has begun adding cards in handwriting you don’t recognize, and today’s card is titled “For when you finally ask.” What does it say?
The bus on your usual route has begun stopping at a station with no name, and today the driver looked at you and waited. Do you get off?
The pond behind your office freezes overnight into a different shape every morning, and today it is your street's exact outline. What is it pointing to?
The community garden’s scarecrow has started changing its hat each night, and this morning it’s wearing yours. What is it warning you about?
The coat-check at the old theater keeps handing out a coat you never left, and its pockets hold a ticket for tonight. Where does it admit you?
The weather vane on the old schoolhouse points at a different front door every dawn, and this morning it's yours. What does it know?
Every umbrella left at the café has started finding its way back to its owner's door by morning, except one, which has been waiting on yours. Who sent it?
The ferry on your river has started docking at a bank that wasn't there yesterday, and the ferryman says only you were expected. Who told him?
The town clock has started striking a thirteenth hour each night, and this evening the whole street stepped outside to wait for it. What are they waiting for?
Your neighbor's wind chimes have started playing a different song each dusk, and tonight it's the lullaby you only ever hummed alone. Who taught it to them?
The lighthouse in your town has started blinking in time with your footsteps, and tonight the keeper left the door open for you. What is it guiding home?
Your local newspaper’s crossword has begun including clues about your day, and today’s final clue, seven letters, reads “what you’ll decide at noon.” What fits?
The corner pharmacy keeps filling a prescription in your name for a medicine that doesn't exist yet, labeled “take when you remember.” What is it for?
A tide table for a town two hundred miles inland arrives at the post office each morning, and today it lists a high tide at your house at four. What is rising?
The pigeons in your square have started lining up facing a different window each morning, and today it's yours, each holding one button. What are they returning?
Every piano in town has drifted a half-step flat overnight, and tonight yours played a single note by itself. What is it tuning toward?
The old toll booth on your road now accepts only things you haven't been given yet, and today the attendant is waiting. What do you offer?
The corner bakery leaves one loaf unsold each evening, labeled with a name that changes nightly, and tonight it's yours. Who is it being saved for?
Your umbrella has started opening itself whenever someone nearby is about to hear bad news, and it just opened beside a stranger. Do you tell them?
Your tape measure has started reading in units nobody can name, and today it says the distance from your front door to home is eleven. Eleven what?
Every snowfall leaves a single line of footprints in your yard that starts at the fence, and each winter it reaches one step nearer your door. Who is walking?
Every sweater you knit this winter comes off the needles with a third sleeve, and this morning a neighbor asked if it was ready. Who is it for?
Lost-pet posters around town now show animals nobody owns, and this morning's has the dog you imagined as a child. Where has it been?
Every leaf that falls in your yard this autumn lands with a single word written on it, and today's raked pile finally finishes a sentence. What does it say?
The yard-sale jigsaw puzzle is always one piece short, and each morning the gap shows a different corner of your living room. What is it waiting to show you?
The secondhand typewriter on your desk types normally all day, but at midnight one key strikes on its own, a single letter each night. What is it spelling?
The parking meter outside your building counts down for a car that never comes, and each evening it expires the moment you get home. Whose time is it keeping?
The attic radio tunes itself each dusk to a station that broadcasts only applause, and tonight it swelled the moment you walked in. What are they applauding?
The snow globe on your windowsill now holds a tiny town that rearranges itself overnight, and this morning one window is lit. Who lives there?
Every jar in your pantry relabeled itself overnight with a year instead of its contents, and the one marked with your birth year is warm. What's inside?
The thermostat in your new apartment refuses to drop below a setting someone chose years ago, and tonight it nudged up one degree on its own. Who's still cold?
The doormat at your new house changes its greeting each morning, and today it says “Welcome back” for the first time. When were you here?
The library book you returned last week came back in your mailbox with margin notes answering questions you only thought while reading. Who’s been reading along?
Your houseplant leans toward whichever room someone is about to enter, and tonight it's turned to face the front door you locked an hour ago. Who's arriving?
Your kitchen kettle has started whistling a different name each morning, and today it whistled your street's old name, the one no map remembers. Who is it calling?
Every seed packet in your garden sprouts something other than its label, and today the row marked carrots grew a wooden chair. What's planted in the next row?
